name: Chonluten

lead: Chonluten (Glu-Asp-Gly) is a short peptide from the Khavinson bioregulator family, associated with the mucosal lining of the airways. People use it for respiratory and general health rather than for a particular look.

The chain runs from support of airway mucosa to easier breathing to better general health. A 2022 cell-line study tested it with other Khavinson peptides for effects on proliferation and inflammatory pathways in cultured monocyte/macrophage cells. No human trial was found.

paras: It is taken in periodic courses within peptide-bioregulator routines, often alongside other Khavinson peptides. Users generally describe it as a background health addition with no specific timeline.
No human safety data was found. It is sold as a research peptide rather than an approved medicine, so quality and legal status vary.

angle.text: Chonluten is promoted in peptide-bioregulator communities as an airway and lung mucosa peptide, used for respiratory and general health rather than a specific look. It has been tested in cultured immune cells; no appearance use has been studied.

lead: Chonluten is a short synthetic peptide with the sequence Glu-Asp-Gly (EDG), one of the Khavinson peptides marketed as peptide bioregulators. It is described as a regulator of the respiratory mucosa, and people in anti-aging and peptide communities discuss it alongside other Khavinson peptides as part of regimens aimed at healthier ageing and a younger appearance.[1][2]

Khavinson peptides are named for Vladimir Khavinson, a Russian gerontologist (1946 to 2024) who directed the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and developed what he called bioregulating peptide therapy. Wikipedia credits him with six peptide pharmaceuticals and dozens of supplements, and presents his claims of slowing ageing as his own; it also notes that much of the sourcing is self-published and that the article cites no independent clinical trials supporting them.[2]

Published evidence found on Chonluten itself is limited to cell-culture work: a 2022 study in a human monocyte/macrophage cell line tested Chonluten together with Epitalon, Vilon, Thymogen and Thymalin for effects on proliferation and inflammatory pathways.[1] No human clinical trial was found, and no study addresses appearance.

paras: The Khavinson peptides were characterised by Vladimir Khavinson from 1973 onward, initially isolated from animal tissues and found to be organ specific, and later made as synthetic short peptides.[1] Chonluten is the tripeptide in this family associated with the bronchial and respiratory lining.[1]

Khavinson directed the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology; the peptide medicines credited to him were first used for military medical personnel exposed to radiation or toxic substances, according to Wikipedia.[2]

Wikipedia reports that Khavinson's work claimed to slow ageing and extend human lifespan and that the peptides have no toxic or adverse effects, presenting these as the author's claims rather than established results; its article flags promotional content and notes the absence of independent clinical trials.[2]

In the 2022 International Journal of Molecular Sciences study, five Khavinson peptides, including Chonluten, were assessed in the THP-1 human monocytic leukemia cell line, which can be differentiated into macrophage-like cells, as regulators of proliferation and inflammation.[1] The findings are in vitro and do not show effects in people.
No studies found. Related work is limited to the cell-line study described above.[1]

timeline.event: Khavinson begins characterising the peptides later grouped as Khavinson peptides.[1]
Chonluten and four other peptides compared in a THP-1 cell-line study.[1]
